event_model_payload.headline: Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave’s First Hour Is Wild
event_model_payload.summary:
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an epic intertwining story set in an Age of Antiquity that most closely resembles Ancient Greece. But! It is also a guns-blazing shiny metal futuristic sci-fi story, and judging by the social media reactions, a lot of people weren't exactly prepared for how hard it leans into that element right from the start. 

In the interest of not spoiling the game and abiding by certain embargo restrictions, we had to say mum about the first hour of Fortune's Weave when previews were published in August. By then it felt like a secret we were all sitting on, especially when a Fire Emblem-themed Nintendo Direct aired and didn't make even the slightest mention of how absolutely buckwild the first hour is. The review embargo was a little looser and I was able to mention in my Fortune's Weave review that the story essentially begins in the future. Even still, Nintendo and Intelligent Systems commit hard to the bit, and for those used to a more fantasy-based Fire Emblem, it can be jarring.

When you start this game you construct your version of Eshmel, Herald of the Pale Raven. Eshmel is essentially a living weapon made to battle the Demon King hordes. The supporting cast are the last remnants of humanity driven to the brink of extinction, fighting a hopeless war. Everything is glowing and futuristic, and characters have weapons that look and function exactly like guns--though they call them Salamanders. It's as if Fire Emblem got a sudden injection of cyberpunk. 

What's more, in your very first tutorial battle, the Demon King summons the Flame Lords against you. Cai, Dietrich, Theodora, and Leda are there, all with a telltale evil, purple glow. This is before the game has mentioned them in any way as the main protagonists, so if you haven't been following the advertising and you're going in totally cold--like I was when I first started it for my preview--this is a striking twist. You know from the start not just that Eshmel has to recruit the Flame Lords to humanity's side, but also, that if you don't, they'll end up working for the Demon Lord instead. Talk about stakes. 

Fans are getting their hands on Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave now, and the reactions to the first Fire Emblem to include guns--err, sorry, Salamanders--is something to watch. Check out a few of the reactions below:

"Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a sprawling masterpiece of a strategy RPG, building upon the successes of past Fire Emblem games with new interconnected elements, expertly designed combat puzzles, and an emphasis on flexibility and choice," I wrote in my review. "Nintendo and Intelligent Systems have topped themselves, making this the new high point to beat for future entries."

event_model_payload.headline: Here’s The Great New Tactics Game You Should Be Playing–And I Don’t Mean Fire Emblem Or Zero Company
event_model_payload.summary:
I've been loving Star Wars Zero Company, especially for how it builds on my favorite story arc from The Clone Wars animated series. But whereas I was positive that Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave would be the title to finally pull me away from Zero Company, it's another tactics game that has captured my attention: Ex Sanguis.

It's no real surprise why I'm enjoying Lightbulb Crew's Ex Sanguis. While it's not a direct sequel to the studio's debut title, Othercide (one of my favorite games of 2020), Ex Sanguis has the same memorable visual style consisting of simple grayscale and striking crimson, a party of heroes who are all elegant women, and turn-based bloodbaths that satisfyingly reward triggering chain events. Ex Sanguis just feels like more Othercide, much in the same way Hollow Knight Silksong and Marvel's Spider-Man 2 feel like extensions to their respective predecessors.

Ex Sanguis has enraptured me so completely with how it differs from Othercide, however. Both tactics games have roguelike elements, but Ex Sanguis really leans into that genre's trappings to offer a snappier gameplay loop. You can boot up the game, play for 20-30 minutes, and feel good for accomplishing a few small victories that will benefit your future attempts. That's not really the case for Othercide, which is designed first and foremost as a brutally challenging tactics game.

Othercide sees you commanding an army of your daughters. Each day, you send a squad of three on a mission in hopes of unlocking a node at the end of the week, leveling up your units to unlock more permanent upgrades. If one dies, she and her perks are gone for good and the only way to replenish one daughter's health is to sacrifice another. Birthing new daughters costs valuable resources. This culminates in a loop of sacrificing units (some of which you've put a lot of time into) for the good of the mission. It's like playing a game like XCOM or Zero Company with permadeath on and purposively leaning into the tragedy of losing a beloved unit.

So while it's very much a tactics game, Othercide has a roguelike feel--from the jump, it's clear that you're not going to do well on your first time trying to unlock a node and face a boss, and you'll need to slowly accrue enough permanent upgrades to enough units to get strong enough to even have a chance at success. And if all your daughters die (which will surely happen more than once), then you're done for and have to start again.

Othercide is a long and arduous grind, one soothed by the intriguing lore that twists between each level and drip-feeds answers to the mystery of what your daughters are and why you're hellbent on sacrificing them to carve and shoot your way to whatever is at the end of all this violence. The game is perfect for folks who like to min-max, but even your best-laid plans can fail if the random nature of the changing levels between each failed attempt screws you over while you're trying to build up an ideal team for the boss at the end. And that can be really frustrating, so it's also a game for those with either a ton of time or a lot of patience.

Ex Sanguis, meanwhile, leans further into the roguelike formula by streamlining everything to make the overall gameplay easier. Each run is substantially shorter than those in Othercide, so getting to some sort of checkpoint is less intense, and it's easier to say, "Okay, one more run" after a failed attempt. The warriors under your command (they're called stillae, rather than daughters, in this game) heal between each mission, and new stillae spawn in automatically between missions if one falls in battle. And each stillae has a choice of one upgrade from three possible options after every mission instead of two, increasing your chances of replicating your favorite builds (and a limited-use re-roll feature to get rid of any options you absolutely hate raises those chances even more).

Ex Sanguis puts a greater onus on completing runs quickly to build up your party and then tackle a boss, while Othercide is all about perfecting how you play a tactics game (and scrapping a run partway through if the randomness of the roguelike elements screw you over on the permadeath mechanic) to have any chance of even holding your own against a boss. Ex Sanguis encourages you to earn a bunch of small victories on your way to each of the big victories, while Othercide is just all about those big victories and being okay with failing a whole bunch between each one. 

Structurally, Ex Sanguis still pretty closely copies Othercide, but I'm no longer drowning in despair at 3 AM because I bungled my latest run, lost my strongest daughters, and now I'm basically starting over from square one.

And like Othercide, Ex Sanguis is a fantastic tactics game. Time is the major factor in every battle. Each action that one of your stillae can take consumes a set number of points from the total pool they have--moving a great distance costs more points than only a few steps, for example, and weaker, fast attacks tend to be cheaper than stronger ones. If a stillae only uses half her total points on her turn, her turn ends as normal. However, you can command each of your warriors to go beyond her limits and use the second half of her points to perform extra actions. Doing so puts the stillae in a bad way, pushing her next turn further back on the overall timeline of the battle as she needs longer to recover. 

Success in a fight is often only rewarded by carefully considering how often to risk pushing any of your stillae in this way, as well as by stacking specific effects together. Certain environmental hazards can trigger explosive chain reactions, for instance, and some stillae can be equipped with abilities that don't act immediately on the overall timeline or only occur if a specific trigger happens, like an enemy wandering into melee range or a nearby stillae reducing a foe's health below a specific threshold. This encourages you to not only think through what you plan on doing next but how each of the various enemies are going to move and attack.

It's a complex series of considerations to keep in mind that only grows as new enemy types are introduced and you unlock more stillae abilities. But setting everything up in just the right way to pinball bounce an enemy into oblivion is so deeply satisfying, much in the same way I've adored Creature in the Well and Marvel's Midnight Suns.

That isn't to say Ex Sanguis is a universal improvement upon Othercide--for as much as this game improves Othercide's gameplay, it drops the ball on narrative. Othercide drips with a horrific gothic atmosphere. Its dark and foreboding story of a mother desperately attempting to utilize her womanhood to save a broken world suffering under a growing fracture in reality is deliciously cryptic--the type of convoluted mystique that's such a delight for theorists to unravel via soothing narration in a YouTube lore video. You piece the story together through snippets of lore dropped in dialogue and by unlocking codex pages, and even then the final result is up to interpretation. It's a challenging game to understand, and subsequently the difficulty of clawing your way through its gameplay emulates that struggle for understanding. Othercide's vibes are perfect.

In comparison, Ex Sanguis doesn't really have a story. There's very little lore provided and no codex to be seen. And while the narrator implies that the stillae are struggling against something, that challenge isn't reflected in the gameplay. I can feel the existence of a narrative, but nothing in the game is focusing it into some sort of recognizable tale.

Admittedly, that all could come later. Ex Sanguis launched into early access with only the first three bosses available and an initial handful of difficulty settings (I've done everything in about six hours), so the full game might tell a more interesting story.

Regardless, if you like tactics games, you should play Ex Sanguis. Well... you should play Othercide first and wonder how you missed it back in 2020. And then you should play Ex Sanguis--maybe it will have gotten a story update by then!

event_model_payload.headline: 007 First Light Just Got Its Biggest Update Yet, And You Can Get It At Its Lowest Price Ever Right Now
event_model_payload.summary:
The history of James Bond games is a little wonky. GoldenEye 007 remains a landmark in gaming history, marking one of the best FPS games of all time almost 30 years ago. Everything or Nothing was a solid classic, but for every good game featuring the MI6 agent, there are some bad ones. Now, I’m not naming names, but I’m specifically looking at 007 Legends and 007 Racing—which, despite the name, isn’t a racing game. Fortunately, IO Interactive’s 007 First Light is firmly on the good side, standing alongside the N64’s GoldenEye as one of the more memorable Bond games, and with a huge update, it’s now cheaper than ever, too.

I know you might want to say (Dr.) No to this deal, but let me sell you on why 007 First Light is one of this year’s best games. Firstly, it’s a pseudo-prequel, which works great as a starting point for newcomers (the last movie was five years ago, after all), while for fans, it offers another interpretation of the beloved double-0 agent. The cinematic aspect basically makes it feel like a new Bond movie, but the gameplay also lives up to the iconic name.

As a globe-trotting adventure, 007 First Light sees James Bond go from a young man with a bad attitude to the familiar shaken-martini drinker we all know and love. Missions offer a mixture of linear, action-packed sequences and open-ended, more sandbox-style levels that fans of IO Interactive’s Hitman series have come to know and love. The awesome Q-Gadgets add another layer of strategy, whether you decide to go in and kill every enemy or take the stealthy approach and leave no trace.

It is, to put it frankly, one of the best action games in recent years. It’s like Uncharted and Hitman had a baby with Daniel Craig, and it’s a perfect blend. If you happen to own one of the best graphics cards right now, you can also enjoy the latest update, which brings Path Tracing to the game. At the very least, my PC is going to hum and then explode like a James Bond gadget, and can any game be more immersive than that?

Right now, you can grab a Steam key for 007 First Light for just $51.09 / £43.79 at Fanatical, a 27% discount off the listed price and the lowest the game has been so far. You won’t want to Buy (it) Another Day, so make sure you grab it while you can. Don’t worry, you’ve got a Licence to Buy (it). Sorry.

So, whether you’re a James Bond fanatic or someone looking for a new game to play, 007 First Light is a perfect opportunity, especially when you can grab it at a discount.

event_model_payload.headline: Scientists Discovered A New Cat Before Rockstar Could Finish GTA 6
event_model_payload.summary:
Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has been in development since 2015, and a lot of things have happened since then, including the recent discovery a new species of cat.

The scientific journal Current Biology disclosed the discovery of Leopardus tilcayo--known as the tilcayo tiger cat--this week. The adorable little creature is smaller than your typical housecat, featuring spots and round ears. According to the discovery, the cat species was found in the Bolivian Yungas forest.

The tilcayo tiger cat is the first new cat species discovered in over 100 years.

Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a co-author of the report, told NBC News that it is currently unknown how many of the cats remain in the wild. She said she discovered the cat basically by accident. She volunteers at a wildlife rehab facility close to La Paz, Bolivia and noticed a tiny cat that she thought was a kitten.

The cat was brought to the facility by a man who was caring for it, feeding it rice and eggs, and later giving it up when he was unable to care for it. Genetic testing was undertaken, and it was discovered that it was indeed a brand-new species of cat never before discovered or documented.

As for more gaming-related things that have happened since GTA 5 came out, GameSpot recently assembled a collection of some of the biggest news stories, including Halo coming to PlayStation, the release of 15+ Call of Duty games, the entire run of Phil Spencer as Xbox CEO, and more.

The wait for GTA 6 has been so long that it's spawned the, “We got ___ before GTA VI” meme. Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick said he is aware of these memes. “I’ve seen some of those," he said.

event_model_payload.headline: Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave Tones Down The Romance
event_model_payload.summary:
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a masterpiece of a Fire Emblem game, but one beloved element that fans of the series have grown attached to is missing in action this time around--or at least, very downplayed.

Romance has been a staple of the Fire Emblem series for years, especially since Fire Emblem Awakening lets you couple up characters and then access the next generation of their children. Three Houses and Engage continued this tradition to a more limited degree, letting your player-character choose a special someone to share a bond with, and watching other characters pair with their highest support levels. By comparison, Fortune's Weave takes a step back from this.

Fortune's Weave does include a robust support system for recruiting characters and accenting their combat abilities, so you'll still see relationships building between the four main Flame Lords, their retinue of companions, and various other recruitable characters. When looking to recruit a character for combat, you'll need to meet a certain level of Renown, a universal stat that expresses your fame and reputation, along with Support with a given character. You can earn more Support by giving gifts and inviting them to special events like meals, visits to the bath house, and plays.

All of this will build your Support level, but there aren't S-tier conversations, and those interactions are only flirtatious at most. Most notably, couples won't pair off romantically.

That's not to say that Fortune's Weave is asexual, however. The characters do have their own romantic lives and the writing recognizes this in the story. As a teenage boy, Cai is a sweet kid who gets teased by older characters about his crushes. Sirocco is a shameless lothario who flirts with just about everyone, and other characters will casually talk about his hookups. Some characters hint at having same-sex attractions, so there's light queer representation. And of course, the presence of a bathhouse means you can technically see them all in their bathing suits. But those are all presented as parts of the characters themselves, not relationships that you can steer towards your desired goals. 

You also can't really go on face-to-face dates with your party members, as you could in previous Fire Emblem games. That system is replaced with a similar system in which your chosen Flame Lord talks with Eshmel, your player-created character. But Eshmel is represented by a white bird nicknamed the Pale Raven when visiting the past Flame Lords, so it's not exactly presented as a romance.

In the context of the story, romance taking a backseat makes sense. This all takes place during a massive tournament, and each of the four Flame Lord heroes has their own motivation for participating that has nothing to do with finding a partner. Similarly, Eshmel is essentially a futuristic construct made to prevent the impending apocalypse, so it might seem odd to have them partner up with a normal human. 

So if you come to Fire Emblem primarily hoping to play matchmaker, Fortune's Weave will likely leave you disappointed. It's a fantastic Fire Emblem game, but it does deemphasize the dating-sim aspect that fans enjoyed in previous entries.

event_model_payload.headline: Gears Of War: E-Day On PC Won’t Let You Play Without A Ray Tracing-Capable GPU
event_model_payload.summary:
Ahead of its release next month, the official PC specs for Gears of War: E-Day have been revealed. The next game in the series has looked good in recent previews, and if you're aiming to reach a high level of fidelity, you're going to need some fairly chunky PC hardware for 4K gibs and perfect reloads. The good news is that no matter which graphics preset you choose, you'll only need 16GB of RAM--welcome news considering just how much memory costs in the current tech climate.

One thing worth pointing out is that graphics cards without dedicated ray-tracing hardware aren't supported. It's not the first time this has been the case--Indiana Jones and the Great Circle being a prime example--but it does create a hard generational lock for interested players. By making ray-tracing hardware a baseline requirement, the game completely phases out massively popular GPUs like the GTX 1060 or AMD's RX 5000 series, making the RTX 2060 the absolute minimum threshold for playing the new Gears of War.

Developer The Coalition says it has continued to iterate and improve PC stability and performance across a wide range of hardware configurations since July, and if you're aiming to run the game at 1080p and 60fps, you'll need a GPU like an Nvidia GeForce RTX 2060, an entry-level RTX 5050, or an AMD Radeon RX 6600 with 6GB of VRAM. Hitting the 1440p 60fps sweet spot increases the hardware requirements to GPUs with 8GB of VRAM, while running the game at 4K 60fps means you'll need a 12GB GeForce RTX 5070 Ti or an AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT.

It's also worth noting that a solid-state drive is required for the game's installation files, and you'll need to free up 115GB of storage space on it. Across the presets, you can expect support for upscaling technology like Nvidia DLSS 4.5, AMD FSR 4, and Intel XeSS 3.0T, which will ease the burden on your PC. The Coalition added that the game includes a benchmark tool to help you fine-tune how it runs on your system.

Gears of War: E-Day PC Requirements

Launching on October 6 for Xbox Series X|S and PC, and day one on Xbox Game Pass, Gears of War: E-Day chronicles the first disastrous encounter between the humans living on the world of Sera and the Locust. The developers behind it recently spoke to GameSpot about a wide range of topics, from solving lore problems to how you strip the flesh off of enemies in the game's new take on Horde mode, and it looks like there's even a Smash Mouth-inspired achievement that you can earn if you want to be a real all-star.

event_model_payload.headline: Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave – Which Flame Lord Should You Pick First?
event_model_payload.summary:
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a sprawling tale composed of four different interconnected heroes, each with their own story campaign. These can be played in any order, and the choice might seem daunting. Which hero is the best to start your journey with? The simple answer is that you can begin with any hero you choose, but if you want to make an informed choice about which one might work best for your tastes, we can help.

After a brief prologue, you're taken to the Obelisk Chamber, where you'll see the obelisks to the four Flame Lords. Those are your passageways into their individual stories. What sets the Flame Lords apart are their special questlines, their Blaze Arts, and their surrounding cast. While you have a great deal of flexibility in recruiting new soldiers to your side and steering your party members in any direction, they are mostly built to excel at particular class types and that will define the type of parties you build with each. 

The Starter Option: Cai

You can think of Cai as the starter character. His special quests grant renown a little more quickly than the others, and so he has an easier time recruiting party members. His Blaze Art is one of the most powerful, an area-of-effect attack that can hit multiple enemies at once, which is a rarity in Fortune's Weave. And his map is more restricted than any of the other Flame Lords, letting you get a feel for how map exploration works without it becoming too dauntingly large and complex. 

Cai's story is similarly made to ease you into the world. Cai is just a kid, so he's not involved in the complex politics of Dagda and the surrounding regions. His goal in the Heroic Games is to free his father, who has been falsely imprisoned. So during his path you'll meet other characters and get a general sense of the sequence of events during the Heroic Games, but it's all very digestible. 

Thus, both from a mechanical and story perspective, choose Cai if you want to ease into Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave. 

For Combat Lovers: Dietrich

Dietrich is a bit more complex, and aimed at getting in reps with the combat system. His special quest is all about finding formidable opponents to fight, which means you can gain lots of combat experience (and valuable experience points) while also getting renown for recruitment. His Blaze Art emphasizes movement and positioning, allowing him to close gaps quickly on an opponent. He can also learn a wide variety of Combat Arts, giving him a ton of combat versatility. And his map opens up fully to let him find faraway opponents to fight, so it will feel like an expansion if you played Cai's story first. He can also summon enemies to fight close to his current location, so you're never far from a battle with Dietrich.

Dietrich's story is also relatively simple. His sword needs blood, so he needs strong opponents and monsters to fight to feed it. There are pieces of political intrigue in his story, as in all the Flame Lords stories, but his personal motivation is plainly just to fight the biggest, baddest people around.

That makes Dietrich ideal for those who love Fire Emblem combat, or who want to get lots of combat reps in. 

Best For Vets: Theodora 

Theodora is the most complex of the combat-focused characters. Her special quest involves scouring the world for supplies to send back home in order to gain renown, so you'll need to do a lot of map exploration and more careful time management to boost your numbers. She also has exclusive access to Gambits, which allows you to assign squadrons of fighters to specific types of units. You can also send recruits out on scouting missions for supplies. Her Blaze Art is straightforward by comparison--she just grabs a gigantic chunk of rock and chucks it across the battlefield, giving her unparalleled attack range. That's partly because, broadly speaking, Theodora and her companions lean the most toward tank-focus, making for slower movement across the battlefield. 

Theodora's story is also among the most complex. As a queen of a neighboring nation, she has the most personal stake in the political machinations of Dagsion, and her story includes lots of proper nouns and discussions of past conflicts. 

All of this means Theodora is best for Fire Emblem veterans, or those who just want to jump in with both feet.

For Support Players: Leda

Finally, Leda is a very different type of character, with an emphasis on support. Her Blaze Arts are a series of dances that grant passive benefits to allies, and her retinue of surrounding cast members are more slanted toward spell-slingers than regular combat units. Her special quest involves traveling the world to perform at different taverns, so you'll need to uncover a lot of the map to find your way to all of the locations. She can also get insider tips on secret spots of the map that only she can access. 

Leda saw her father slaughtered in front of her and made it her life's mission to find the man who killed him and exact revenge. Her story is therefore extremely personal, and while she witnesses some of the political intrigue in and around Dagsion, she doesn't really care about it beyond how it impacts her quest for vengeance. She practically floats outside of the main events of the story because she's so single-minded to her goal.

Leda is best if you want to play support and experience a more personal story.

Or, Just Jump Around

So in broad terms, the characters are essentially ordered left-to-right to give you a smooth path through the game, if you take them in that order: Cai to ease you into the world and mechanics, Dietrich to get a lot of combat experience, Theodora to build on the others' combat and story complexity, and Leda to round it out with support and a more personal story.

However, all of the paths start on the easier side and slowly ramp up, so you won't feel too overwhelmed taking on any of them first. You should pick whichever Flame Lord interests you the most. And you can always switch to a different Flame Lord at almost any point, so there's no reason you can't hop around or even play their chapters one at a time for each.

event_model_payload.headline: I Played WoW: Forever On A Controller, And That’s Big News
event_model_payload.summary:
World of Warcraft: Forever, Blizzard's next evolution of WoW Classic that will see significant changes and content additions, is fully playable on controller.

I got to experience WoW: Forever's new Skyborne elf starting zone with the control scheme during a hands-on demo at BlizzCon 2026. A prompt outlining the controls noted controller support was in an "alpha" state, but despite supposedly still being in early development, it worked surprisingly well.

That's a first for Blizzard's MMORPG. Though Blizzard has added barebones support for controllers in recent years, an entirely mouse-and-keyboard-free setup relies on unofficial, player-made add-ons like ConsolePort to deliver a true console-like experience.

From what I played at BlizzCon, Blizzard adding a fully featured controller option could be a game-changer. Despite having played WoW on a mouse and keyboard for 22 years, I was shocked at how natural it felt. Cycling through friendly or enemy NPCs is done with the shoulder buttons. Interacting and jumping are done with the face buttons. Abilities and spells are bound to both the d-pad and the face buttons, with additional keybinds accessible by pressing one or both triggers. Each trigger provides access to eight keybinds, with another eight from holding down both triggers at the same time. Combined with the d-pad, you have 28 buttons at your fingertips. 

That sounds like a lot of buttons, but in some scenarios, particularly in WoW Classic or WoW: Forever, it might not be enough. Certain classes, particularly spellcasters, are notorious for having access to an almost comical number of skills and abilities in WoW Classic. This is largely due to many spells having multiple ranks, with lower ranked versions doing less damage or healing but also costing less mana. That makes them still useful in certain situations, but definitely clutters up one's action bars.

Outside of the actual basics of using combat abilities and talking to NPCs, WoW: Forever's controller support felt a little more cumbersome. On keyboard and mouse, opening your inventory is as easy as hitting the "b" key and then clicking what you want. On a controller, it requires bringing up a radial menu, sliding over to the inventory section, and then cycling through all the items in your bag until you reach the one you're looking for. Considering players can have dozens of items in their bags at once, trying to select what you want definitely feels slower and less straightforward than is ideal.

Ultimately, full controller support for WoW: Forever might be more suited for some classes or particular playstyles over others. The modern "retail" version of WoW, currently in the middle of its most recent Midnight expansion, would arguably benefit from controller support even more than WoW Classic or Forever. Modern WoW generally has fewer buttons to press and less inventory management to do, and I could see this controller setup working wonders for those who want to run some delves on their couch or casually complete world quests.

Blizzard's full plans for WoW controller support aren't currently clear. The demo labeled controller support as an alpha, and Blizzard announced during the show Forever will be fully playable with a controller come launch on November 4. It made no announcements regarding if the feature will eventually come to retail, though considering how much DNA is now being shared between the multiple versions of WoW, it seems safe to assume it will. GameSpot has reached out to Blizzard for comment and clarification about its plans for controller support, and will update this post if we hear back.

The elephant in the room is whether Blizzard's controller initiative will pave the way for an eventual console version. Blizzard is, of course, currently owned by Microsoft, the owner of Xbox. Fans have speculated given WoW: Midnight's user-made add-on restrictions (something that will carry over into Forever) and its pruning of many class abilities last year that Blizzard was setting the table for a console version.

It wouldn't be too shocking to see WoW at long last make its debut on Xbox, though Blizzard made clear last year that if it were making a console version, it would tell fans about it. Handheld PCs, including Xbox-branded ones, are also more popular than ever before, and WoW receiving full controller support would open the way for the MMO to be officially playable on those devices as well.

Regardless of whether a console version eventually happens, having a fully functioning controller option still feels long overdue from a simple accessibility standpoint on PC. Seeing that Blizzard is finally hard at work delivering one is nothing but good news. From what I played, it's simple, intuitive, and perhaps even easier in some ways than playing on mouse and keyboard, though I'm sure there are scenarios, like inventory management, where it might leave something to be desired. Whatever Blizzard's full plans for controller support are, it can't come soon enough.

event_model_payload.headline: "If the player trusts you enough, they are not going to savescum": Why the makers of some of the best RPGs on PC want you to get used to failing
event_model_payload.summary:
When it comes to RPGs, I am an irredeemable savescummer. I admit it. I'll slam F9 at the drop of a hat (perhaps the hat was dropped as a result of a failed dexterity roll. Unacceptable. Reload).

So when I recently found myself reloading a Divinity 2 save for the umpteenth time in a single session, I started to wonder - in a genre that's supposedly about storytelling first and foremost, why am I viewing botched persuasion checks as something to be studiously avoided? And why is it that I feel totally different about making a horrible mess of things in tabletop roleplaying games?

After all, some of my fondest memories of real-life roleplaying are moments of extravagant failure: sometimes of the bathetic stepping-on-a-rake-instead-of-slaying-the-necromancer variety, and sometimes of the much more grounded, human, and affecting type.

It all got me thinking: how do RPG developers think about player failure? Would they recognise the distinction between digital and tabletop that I'm describing? And can they convince a savescummer like me to renounce my ways?

event_model_payload.headline: What are we all playing this weekend?
event_model_payload.summary:
I’m a big fan of these September weekends where I wake up and my bedroom has neither the humidity nor the ambient temperature of an Eden Project rainforest-o-dome. Autumn was previously my third favourite season at best, but I think we need to have a serious conversation about top two.

The additional thermal headroom to comfortably run a toasty graphics card also makes this one of the better times to play games. Including these, and also, the ones you’re going to tell us about in the comments.
